title: Tamil Shaivism and the Tevaram
hook: a king summons a temple singer, and Appar sends back a song instead

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tamil Shaivism and the Tevaram: Sundarar, stopped at his own wedding, whose first hymn begins with the word he shouted, madman. This week ran from Lal Ded in Kashmir to these hymns in the south. Did a sharp word turn kinder before it landed? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-two.

A messenger arrives with an order from the king: come to court. The man being summoned is a singer of Shiva, carrying a small hoe, the kind used to pull grass from between the stones of a temple courtyard. The stories call him Appar. He hears the order out. Then, instead of packing a bag, he answers with a song. Its opening, in paraphrase: we are subjects of no one, and we do not fear death. The messenger goes back to the palace carrying a hymn instead of a prisoner. Today, Appar, and the song he sent back.
screen: `AN ORDER FROM THE KING.` → `AN OLD MAN WITH A HOE.` → `A SONG SENT BACK.`

segments.voice: First, the summons. Appar's life is told in the Periya Puranam, the book of the lives of the Shaiva saints of the Tamil country. It says he spent a long time on another path and then came home to Shiva, and that the king was angry about it. So the order to come to court is not an invitation. It's a threat. Now the song. In paraphrase, it says: we are no one's subjects, we do not fear death, we will not suffer in hell, we do not tremble, we know no sickness, we bow to no one, because we belong to the Lord. Turn it once. This isn't a protest against kings in general. It's a statement about ownership. If his whole life belongs to Shiva, there's simply no room left for a second master. Turn it again, and look at the hoe. The man who says he bows to no king spends his days on his knees, pulling weeds out of temple stones so others can walk there barefoot. Free of the palace, and a servant of the courtyard, in the same body. And the story doesn't end with the song. Tradition says the king had him tied to a heavy stone and thrown into the sea, and that Appar sang the five syllables, namah shivaya, and the stone floated him to shore. Some readers take that as a plain miracle; others hear it as a picture of what the name of Shiva can hold up. Either way, notice what he carries into the water: not an argument, a name. On an ordinary day, the song isn't telling anyone to ignore their boss. It's asking a quieter question: under all the voices that summon you, which one do you finally answer to?
screen: `A SUMMONS THAT IS A THREAT` · `SUBJECTS OF NO ONE` · `A HOE FOR THE TEMPLE STONES` · `THE STONE THAT FLOATED`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: finding what you answer to. Sit, and let the breath slow. Notice the voices that summon you today: a message, a deadline, somebody's opinion. Name them one at a time, without pushing them away. Then ask, quietly: under all of these, what do I answer to in the end? Let the answer be a word, a person, a promise, or God. Rest there for the sit. If you pray, you can say the five syllables Appar sang, namah shivaya, slowly, with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Tamil Shaivism and the Tevaram. Today, Appar, the singer with a hoe, who answered a king's summons with a song: we are subjects of no one. Today's word.
screen: `TAMIL SHAIVISM AND THE TEVARAM — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: Tamil Shaivism and the Tevaram. Today, when something summons you in a hurry, take one breath before you answer, and remember who you answer to. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: In Tamil Shaiva temples, singers called oduvars sing hymns of the Tevaram, including Appar's, during worship, and Appar is often shown in images carrying his small hoe.

original.note: Sanskrit: the five syllables, 'bowing to Shiva', which tradition says Appar sang when he was thrown into the sea.

trapdoor: what you thought: Appar was a rebel against a king.
what it means: belonging wholly to Shiva left no room for a second master, while he spent his days weeding temple stones.
what a scholar hears: the Tevaram gathers Appar's hymns with those of Sambandar and Sundarar, and the Periya Puranam tells their lives.

notes: Editor pass: review rewritten to pick up yesterday (Sundarar, madman) as well as the week; 'old singer' cut (no age in the sources used); 'spent years' softened to 'a long time'. Angle checked against 1370–1371: no overlap.

Appar's earlier years on another path (the Jain community, in the Periya Puranam) are deliberately left unnamed so that no tradition is the foil; the persecutors in the hagiography are left as 'the king'. Confirm this framing.

Paraphrase of the nāmārkkum kuṭiyallōm hymn: confirm the list (no one's subjects, no fear of death, no hell, no trembling, no sickness, bow to no one) and its setting as his reply to the royal summons.
The hoe (uzhavarappadai) as Appar's attribute for cleaning temple premises: confirm.
The stone-in-the-sea episode and the Namasivaya hymn connected to it: confirm as told in the Periya Puranam.
